app_claim: A slab of green-grey sandstone about 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m at the foot of the Great Trilithon, from outside southern Britain. Drawn lying flat at ground level.
problem: The vague phrase 'from outside southern Britain' under-states and obscures the strongest current geological evidence: the Altar Stone matches Old Red Sandstone from the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland, at least 750 km from Stonehenge, and cannot have come from southern Britain south of the Iapetus Suture. The exact outcrop remains unresolved, so the correction should say that.

evidence.title: A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge
evidence.what_it_says: Detrital mineral ages and chemistry point to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland; the authors state the Altar Stone 'cannot have been sourced from southern Britain' and infer a transport distance of at least 750 km.

replacements.old: A slab of green-grey sandstone about 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m at the foot of the Great Trilithon, from outside southern Britain. Drawn lying flat at ground level.
replacements.new: A slab of green-grey sandstone about 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m at the foot of the Great Trilithon. Its chemistry most closely matches the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland, at least 750 km away; the exact outcrop remains unresolved. Drawn lying flat at ground level.

replacements.old: Its date of placing is tentative (Darvill: Stage 2, perhaps any time before the Great Trilithon fell on it); its original posture (flat or upright) is not established; its source is unsettled.

app_claim: Lesser Stonehenge Cursus: fresh chalk [-3050 → -2750], built -3000. Context: 'Date: antler c. 3000 BCE (Wikipedia only), which conflicts with EH's centuries around 3500 BC.'
problem: The model resolves a known date conflict in favour of the weaker Wikipedia-only c. 3000 BCE value and displays construction at 3000 BCE. English Heritage explicitly says the Stonehenge and Lesser Cursus were built about 3500 BCE. The app therefore makes the Lesser Cursus roughly half a millennium too late while its own uncertainty text admits the conflict.

app_claim: Coneybury Anomaly feasting pit (date unverified) [year -3800]. Note: 'The date of about 3800 BCE comes from the project brief and was not confirmed in any source read; treat as uncertain.'
problem: The date is now confirmed by an accessible English Heritage source, but the app still labels it unverified and cites only Wikipedia. English Heritage dates the earliest cattle bone from the Coneybury Anomaly to 3950–3790 BCE. The event should cite that source and distinguish the dated bone from the pit's construction date.

app_claim: Amesbury Abbey: 'Fontevraud priory church (form unknown)' [-1177 → -1540], with built=null. Context: 'The 979 church and the 1177 priory church are drawn identically because nothing says the fabric changed.'
problem: The phase makes 1177 look like the date of a priory church in use. The 1177 event was the refoundation; Henry II then had a new house and church built, and the nuns were installed in the new buildings in 1186. The model should therefore treat 1177-1186 as construction and 1186 as completion, while retaining the warning that the actual form is unknown.

replacements.old: The 979 church and the 1177 priory church are drawn identically because nothing says the fabric changed. The date of demolition after the Dissolution is unknown; shown decaying until 1580 as a placeholder.
replacements.new: The 979 church and the later priory church are drawn identically because their form is unknown. The 1177 refoundation was followed by construction of a new house and church, completed by 1186. The date of demolition after the Dissolution is unknown; shown decaying until 1580 as a placeholder.

app_claim: Durrington Walls timber ring [-2490 → -2450], end 'replaced'; Durrington Walls henge: fresh chalk [-2480 → -2430].
problem: The two phases overlap from 2480 to 2450 BCE even though the timber ring is explicitly marked 'replaced' and the henge bank was raised along the same line. Current Archaeology states that the posts were removed and their sockets filled before being covered by the henge. The animation can therefore show a dismantled monument and its successor together for three decades.

evidence.title: Rethinking Durrington Walls: a long-lost monument revealed
evidence.what_it_says: The posts were removed and their sockets filled before being covered by the later henge; the article describes a maximum 50-year window and notes that the henge succeeded the post circle.

app_claim: Durrington Walls houses grow [-2525 → -2505] and decline [-2480 → -2440], while the note says occupation was 'only about 10-12 years ending c. 2500-2460 BCE.'
problem: The site-specific house zone spreads appearance, full presence and disappearance across an 85-year window (2525-2440 BCE), contradicting its own note and the Bayesian/stratigraphic evidence for roughly 10-12 years of occupation. Astra corrected the same over-long interval in the national Durrington place, but this detailed-site zone would still visually imply a multi-decade settlement.

evidence.title: Rethinking Durrington Walls: a long-lost monument revealed
evidence.what_it_says: The underlying Neolithic village is thought to have been inhabited for only 10-12 years, based on house-floor renewals and quarry pits; Bayesian analysis puts its end at c. 2500-2460 BCE.

replacements.old: Eight houses about 5 m square, with clay or chalk floors, central hearths and box-bed and dresser outlines, were excavated inside the later henge on its east side, towards the Avon (2006); modelling puts the village at only about 10-12 years' occupation ending c. 2500-2460 BCE (the 2007 release gave 2600-2500 BCE). The TOTAL NUMBER of houses is not known: 'up to 1000 houses' (Wikipedia) is an upper speculation, 'hundreds of people' the excavators' phrase. About 60 houses (a count chosen to give 'a few dozen') are drawn on a lattice inside the site polygon 'durrington-settlement' (about 1.1 ha on the east side of the enclosure, an approximation); positions are not surveyed. The village was abandoned about when the henge was dug (the ring of posts and the henge bank follow).

app_claim: Woodhenge (six oval rings of timber posts): 'Woodhenge: six oval rings of timber posts' [-2480 → -2350], built -2470; Woodhenge ditch and bank [-2480 → -2400], built -2470.
problem: The model puts both the timber rings and the enclosing henge at about 2470 BCE. Historic England's 2024 chronological modelling dates the timber settings to 2635-2575 cal BC (95%) and the ditch and bank to 2495-2180 cal BC (93%), probably 2465-2345 cal BC. It also concludes that rings A and B had probably decayed before the henge was built, after an interval of probably 145-280 years. The current Woodhenge is therefore roughly a century too late and collapses two distinct construction episodes into one.

evidence.title: Woodhenge, Durrington, Wiltshire: Radiocarbon Dating and Chronological Modelling
evidence.what_it_says: The timber monument was constructed in 2635-2575 cal BC (95% probability); the ditch and bank in 2495-2180 cal BC (93% probability), probably 2465-2345 cal BC; the timber setting was enclosed after probably 145-280 years, by which time rings A and B had probably long since disintegrated.
